title: Queue drain patterns and latency outliers journal
content:
Purpose:
This is a working journal capturing experiments, profiling notes, and micro-benchmarks around an observed class of tail latency outliers tied to 'queue drain' behavior in the continuous-batching scheduler. Goal: identify simple heuristics and guardrails (short-term) and a robust algorithmic mitigation (mid-term) to reduce p99/p999 regressions without hurting throughput.

Background / why this surfaced:
- Multiple customer incidents where p99 increased by ~2-4× under skewed arrival traces.
- Spike pattern: heavy arrival burst then a long sparse tail. Scheduler forms large batches during burst, then small stragglers cause repeated flushes during drain waves.
- Existing timeouts and size thresholds were tuned for steady Poisson-like traffic; they underperform for 'bursty then sparse' workloads.

Instrumentation added this run:
- Per-request enqueue timestamp, batch formation start/end, flush-trigger reason (size/timeout/starvation-window).
- Batch histogram (size, latency), per-core queue occupancy timeline, KV-cache-hit-rate during drain.
- Flamegraphs for scheduler thread and GPU stall samples (1ms sampling).

Measurement harness / test parameters:
- Synthetic replay traces derived from production: two classes (A: bursty 10kqps 500ms window, then 2qps tail for 20s; B: steady 200qps).
- Models: open-llama-7B quantized int8, sequence len 512, greedy decoding 1 token per request to amplify overheads.
- Nodes: 4x V100-equivalent (dedicated dev cluster).
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99/p999, batch_size_distribution, per-request end-to-end, scheduler spin time, GPU utilization.

Key observations (raw):
- Under trace A, p99 increased from 120ms baseline to ~720ms during drain waves. p999 spikes up to 1.8s.
- 65% of p99 outliers are in requests that were flushed due to 'starvation timeout' after being demoted from earlier batch windows.
- Flamegraphs show scheduler spends disproportionate CPU time in list traversal and eviction logic when many tiny batches are formed in rapid succession.
- KV cache pressure: when drain waves interleave with cache misses, per-token GPU time increases ~10-15%, amplifying latency.

Hypotheses generated:
1) Fixed absolute timeout (e.g., 20ms) causes premature flush of partially-filled batches during drain tails; adaptive timeout based on recent arrival rate would reduce unnecessary flushes.
2) Batch formation ordering (FIFO only) fails to pack latency-sensitive short requests that arrive during a drain wave; short-circuit priority or tiny-slot reservation could improve packing without impacting fairness.
3) Thundering small-batch flushes create scheduler CPU overhead — introduce coalescing gate with exponential backoff to prevent repeated flush cycles.

Small experiments run (notes):
- Experiment E1: adaptive timeout = max(10ms, 3 * median_interarrival_5s). Result: p99 reduced ~30% on trace A, throughput unchanged. Some requests saw +10ms tail.
- Experiment E2: reserve one "packing slot" per core to boost assembly of 2-4 request micro-batches; reduced p999 spikes but slightly increased p90 (tradeoff).
- Experiment E3: coalescing-gate (suppress flush if previous flush < X ms ago). Eliminated oscillations but induced rare 500ms waits when combined with long CPU GC pause — needs guard.

Profiles and artifacts (short):
- scheduler_cpu.svg: shows repeated peaks aligned with small-batch flushes.
- batch_size_hist.csv: bimodal distribution during drain (mode 1 at size 1, mode 2 at size 64).
- kv_cache_miss_trace.log: correlated with the worst outliers.

Actionable heuristics we think are low-risk to ship ASAP:
- Adaptive timeout based on short-term interarrival median (window 3-5s, multiplier 2.5-3.5).
- Introduce an anti-oscillation suppression: once a batch flush happens due to timeout, disallow another timeout-based flush on the same queue for at least 2x the timeout value.
- Add instrumentation flags to enable per-tenant 'drain-mode' which toggles packing slot reservation.

Mid-term algorithm ideas (research tracks):
- Predictive drain detector: run a lightweight arrival-rate predictor (EWMA + burst detector) and switch scheduler policy modes (burst-mode vs drain-mode).
- Priority-aware packing with fairness aging: allow very-short requests to be packed ahead if their wait > some small quantile but ensure long requests don't starve.
- Hybrid scheduling: combine size-timeout with opportunistic deferred flush (if GPU utilization above threshold, be more aggressive packing).

Open questions / risks:
- Does adaptive timeout interact badly with tenant QoS SLAs? Need SLO safety checks.
- How do these heuristics interact with multi-model co-location and mixed-seq-length workloads? We saw cases where packing short requests into a large batch caused memory fragmentation and extra kernel launches.
- Edge-case: pause during long GC or OS scheduling caused our suppression gate to hold requests too long. Must include watchdog bypass if scheduler doesn't see progress.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Run adaptive-timeout + packing-slot together on 10/10 replay; capture p999 distribution per-tenant (owner: Ethan).
- [ ] Add watchdog bypass to suppression gate (owner: Marta).
- [ ] Add synthetic mixed-seq experiment (seq lengths 64/512 mixed). (owner: Diego).
- [ ] Draft a small RFC for 'drain-mode' policy and safety rollback plan.

Notes to self:
- Keep experiments small and feature-flagged. We want quick mitigation in prod without full algorithm swap.
- Preserve observability: add a per-flush reason label to metrics (size/timeout/starvation/backoff) so we can alert when drain-mode heuristics are in play.

Appendix: rough numeric snapshot from run E1 (trace A):
- baseline p99: 120ms -> adaptive-timeout p99: 85ms (best-effort median over 5 runs)
- p999 baseline: 1800ms -> adaptive-timeout p999: 680ms
- avg batch size baseline: 28 -> during burst 62, during drain 3 -> adaptive-timeout increased drain avg to 7

If useful I'll convert this into a short playbook and a PR with the adaptive-timeout implementation and instrumentation toggles.
